claims.text: W–Cu composites containing tungsten particles or connected tungsten regions in a copper matrix are typically processed by spark-plasma sintering or mechanical alloying.
A conformal nanometric nickel coating on tungsten particles improves interfacial bonding with a copper matrix.
The nickel coating reduces void formation and phase separation in W–Cu composites.
The nickel coating preserves mechanical durability under irradiation conditions.
A uniform nickel layer approximately 5 nm thick should be deposited on tungsten particles by atomic layer deposition before mixing with copper powder and sintering.
Spark-plasma sintering under vacuum at approximately 900–1000 °C with a controlled hold time can ensure full densification of the Ni-coated W–Cu composite.
An interfacial nickel layer acts as a binder between tungsten and copper.
The nickel interlayer enhances wetting and interdiffusion between tungsten and copper.
Enhanced wetting and interdiffusion improve interparticle contact and reduce interfacial porosity.
The nickel interlayer facilitates diffusional bonding during sintering.
Nickel facilitates bonding by lowering the interfacial-energy mismatch at the tungsten–copper boundary.
Nickel enhances atomic mobility at the tungsten–copper boundary.
Enhanced diffusional bonding produces more uniform W–Cu contact and minimizes void formation and phase segregation.
The large melting- and boiling-point differences between tungsten and copper cause void formation and phase segregation.
Relative to spark-plasma-sintered composites made with uncoated tungsten particles, Ni-coated composites will have higher thermal conductivity.
Relative to uncoated composites, Ni-coated composites will have greater fatigue resistance and less void-related mechanical degradation under simulated irradiation service.
Uncoated W–Cu composites made by conventional spark-plasma sintering or mechanical alloying tend to contain voids and phase separation.
The intervention is effective at processing temperatures up to approximately 1000 °C and under moderate irradiation and thermal cycling typical of fusion-reactor joints.
Extended irradiation or high thermal cycling may destabilize the nickel interlayer.
Brittle intermetallic compounds may form at the interface and counteract the coating's benefits if processing conditions are not optimized.
